name: ADHD Test
tagline: Check how strongly you recognise adult ADHD traits.
intro: This screener looks at four areas linked to ADHD in adults: inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity and executive functioning, such as planning and time management. Answer based on how often each statement has applied to you over the last six months. It takes about five minutes and is not a diagnosis, but it can help you understand your patterns and decide whether to seek an assessment.
seoTitle: ADHD Test: Free adult ADHD screener
seoDescription: Do you struggle with focus, restlessness or planning? Take this 5-minute adult ADHD screener and get a personal report on four key areas.

inattention.name: Inattention
inattention.short: How easily your attention drifts, and how often you lose track of details or things.
inattention.low: Your answers suggest that you can usually keep your attention where you want it. You follow conversations, notice details and keep track of your belongings without much trouble. Everyone gets distracted sometimes, especially when tired or stressed, so occasional lapses are normal. Protect the habits that help you focus, such as enough sleep and limiting interruptions during important work. If your focus changes noticeably, check in with yourself about stress or sleep.
inattention.mid: Your answers suggest that your attention drifts more than you would like in some situations, for example in long meetings, with boring tasks or in busy environments. This can be influenced by stress, sleep and workload as well as by personal style. Try working in short focused blocks, removing distractions such as notifications and writing important things down straight away so your memory does not have to hold everything.
inattention.high: Your answers suggest that keeping your attention on tasks, conversations and details is often a struggle for you, and that forgetfulness may affect your daily life. These are common signs of ADHD in adults, but stress, low mood, anxiety and poor sleep can cause similar problems. Consider talking to a doctor or a qualified professional who can assess what is behind it. In the meantime, external tools like reminders, checklists and fixed places for your belongings can ease the load.

hyperactivity.name: Hyperactivity
hyperactivity.short: How much physical and inner restlessness you experience.
hyperactivity.low: Your answers suggest that you feel fairly calm and settled. Sitting still, waiting or relaxing in your free time does not seem to cause you much tension. That ability to slow down helps with recovery and concentration. Keep including enough movement in your day as well, since physical activity supports both mood and focus. If you ever notice restlessness growing during stressful periods, short walks or breathing exercises can help you reset.
hyperactivity.mid: Your answers suggest a moderate level of restlessness. You may fidget, feel the urge to move or find it hard to switch off at times, especially when you are bored. Regular exercise, short movement breaks and activities that keep your hands busy can help channel this energy. Notice whether restlessness rises with stress or lack of sleep, and adjust where you can.
hyperactivity.high: Your answers suggest that you often feel physically or mentally restless, find it hard to sit still and struggle to relax. In adults, hyperactivity often shows up as inner restlessness and a racing mind rather than running around. These are possible signs of ADHD, although anxiety, stress and other factors can play a role. Consider discussing them with a doctor or a qualified professional. Regular intense exercise and planned movement breaks can bring some relief.

impulsivity.name: Impulsivity
impulsivity.short: How often you act, speak or decide before thinking things through.
impulsivity.low: Your answers suggest that you usually pause before you act or speak. You seem to weigh up decisions, wait your turn and keep your reactions in check. This thoughtful approach protects you from many regrets. Just make sure caution does not stop you from seizing good opportunities when they come along. If you notice that you react more quickly when tired or stressed, that is normal; simply build in a little more rest during busy periods.
impulsivity.mid: Your answers suggest that you sometimes act on impulse, for example by interrupting, buying things on a whim or reacting quickly when annoyed. A bit of spontaneity can be energising, but it helps to build in small pauses. Try a simple rule, such as waiting a day before larger purchases or counting to five before replying in a heated moment.
impulsivity.high: Your answers suggest that you often act, speak or decide before thinking things through, and that this may lead to regrets in money, relationships or work. Strong impulsivity is a common feature of ADHD, but it can also have other causes. Consider talking to a doctor or a qualified professional about what you notice. Practical strategies, such as delaying important decisions and limiting easy access to temptations, can help you feel more in control.

executive.name: Executive function
executive.short: How well you plan, organise, manage time and follow through on tasks.
executive.low: Your answers suggest that planning, organising and managing your time generally go well for you. You seem to get started on tasks, meet deadlines and keep your life in reasonable order. These skills make daily life much smoother. Keep using the systems that work for you, and review them when your responsibilities change. If you share tips with others, you may find your organising strengths are valued more than you think.
executive.mid: Your answers suggest that some areas of organisation and time management cost you extra effort. You may procrastinate on boring tasks, underestimate how long things take or lose track of admin now and then. Simple systems can help a lot: one calendar for everything, breaking tasks into small steps and setting your own earlier deadlines. Reward yourself for finishing, not only for starting.
executive.high: Your answers suggest that planning, starting tasks, managing time and staying organised are often hard for you, and that this may cause stress at work or at home. Difficulties with executive functions are very common in adults with ADHD, but can also come from burnout, depression or overload. Consider talking to a doctor or a qualified professional for an assessment. Coaching, external structure and body doubling, working alongside someone else, help many people get things done.

summary: This screener shows how strongly you recognise four groups of traits associated with ADHD in adults. Higher scores mean more frequent difficulties in that area. The results reflect your own view of the last six months and are not a diagnosis: only a qualified professional can assess ADHD.
